claim: The story that Charles Darwin renounced evolution and embraced Christ on his deathbed traces to 'Lady Hope' (Elizabeth Hope), a British evangelist who told a Massachusetts gathering in 1915 — thirty-three years after Darwin died in 1882 — that she had visited him near the end and found him reading Hebrews and lamenting his theory. Darwin's family, who were actually present at his death, flatly denied it. His daughter Henrietta Litchfield, in print in 1922: 'I was present at his deathbed... He never recanted any of his scientific views, then or earlier.' Darwin died an agnostic, courteous toward faith he did not share, and no serious historian — Christian or otherwise — credits the tale. Notice also that the story would prove nothing even if true: theories stand or fall on evidence, not on their authors' final anxieties; Christianity would not be falsified by a deathbed recantation from Paul's biographer, and evolution is not falsified by one from Darwin. Repeating this legend does double damage: it spreads a falsehood, and it implies the speaker's case needs one.

sources.name: TalkOrigins, 'The Lady Hope Story: A Widespread Falsehood'
Wikipedia, 'Elizabeth Hope' (the legend's history)
Answers in Genesis lists it among arguments to avoid
James Moore, The Darwin Legend (the scholarly autopsy)

response: There is no counter to steelman — the skeptic is right, the historians are right, and even the major creationist organizations agree the story is false. The Darwin family's firsthand denials, the thirty-three-year gap, and the total absence of corroboration settle it. A Christian repeating it is bearing false witness about a dead man, in service of a point that would be logically worthless even if the story were true.
responseSource: James Moore, The Darwin Legend; Henrietta Litchfield's 1922 denial in The Christian
rationale: Don't use, ever. The command against false witness does not have an apologetics exemption. If it comes up, the Christian's move is to debunk it FIRST — nothing builds trust with a skeptic faster than watching a believer kill a convenient legend on principle.
context: The story that Darwin renounced evolution on his deathbed and asked for the Gospel to be preached traces to a woman known as Lady Hope, who claimed to have visited him. Darwin's daughter Henrietta, who was present during his final illness, denied it flatly and in print. The story keeps circulating because it is satisfying. This case treats it as a test case in source-checking: the person you are talking to can disprove it on a phone in twenty seconds, and will then reasonably discount everything else you said.

title: Pascal's wager as an opener: wrong tool, wrong slot
claim: Deployed as a conversation-opener — 'you might as well believe; if you're wrong you lose nothing' — the wager fails three ways, and skeptics know all three. The many-gods objection: the same bet works for Allah, Vishnu, or a deity who rewards honest doubt and punishes hedged belief, so the wager alone selects no religion. The doxastic problem: belief is not a light switch — no one can sincerely believe a proposition for prize money, as the skeptic being lectured is vividly aware while not-believing. The mercenary problem: it presents faith as fire insurance, which misrepresents a Gospel whose call is love of God, not actuarial self-interest. What almost everyone misses is that Pascal knew this. The wager appears in the Pensées aimed at a specific reader: the sophisticated Parisian too indifferent to investigate. Its real function is anti-apathy — to show that the God question is not intellectually optional, that the stakes make honest investigation mandatory — after which Pascal prescribes practice and inquiry, not instant belief. That limited use survives: as a closing nudge to a genuine inquirer ('this question deserves your serious attention'), not as an opening argument to a skeptic.

sources.name: SEP, 'Pascal's Wager' (the objections, formalized)
Blaise Pascal, Pensées (the wager in context, fragment 233)
Wikipedia, 'Pascal's wager' (many-gods objection history)
Peter Kreeft's sympathetic reconstruction (the legitimate limited use)

response: The skeptic's objections are sound against the pop version: the wager is decision theory with a rigged partition (it assumes exactly two live options), it demands belief as an act of will (impossible), and the God it imagines — fooled by self-interested compliance — is not worth believing in; an omniscient being would presumably prefer honest disbelief to strategic pretense. Even the rehabilitated anti-apathy use has a limit: it motivates INQUIRY, and inquiry may honestly conclude against faith — the wager cannot then be re-invoked to overrule the verdict it commissioned.
responseSource: Standard objections catalogued in SEP's 'Pascal's Wager' entry (many-gods; doxastic voluntarism; the mercenary-faith problem)
rationale: Don't use as an opener or as a proof — graded 'answered' because in its common street form the skeptical counters succeed. Salvage: at the END of a conversation with a genuinely undecided person, Pascal's actual point ('this question is too important for indifference — investigate it seriously') is both honest and effective. Slot matters: last word to the apathetic, never first word to the skeptic.
context: Pascal's wager — that betting on God is rational given what is at stake — is a genuinely interesting piece of philosophy, and it was never designed to do the job it is usually given. Pascal aimed it at someone already persuaded the odds were non-trivial and unable to move the final inch. Led with, it lands as an invitation to fake a belief for insurance purposes, which is both poor philosophy and poor theology, and it invites the obvious reply about all the other gods on offer.

title: Mind-reading the atheist: 'you secretly believe,' 'you have no morals,' 'atheism takes more faith'
claim: Three tropes to retire, and Scripture itself retires the worst of them. 'Atheists secretly believe and are suppressing it' proof-texts Romans 1 while ignoring that Romans 2:14-15 says Gentiles without the law 'do by nature what the law requires' because it is 'written on their hearts' — the Bible PREDICTS morally serious, conscience-driven unbelievers; it does not license telling your neighbor she is lying about her own inner life. Empirically, many atheists are deconverts who describe leaving faith as painful, slow, and honest — often through church hurt; telling them their loss was secretly insincere re-opens the wound and ends the conversation. 'Atheists have no basis for morality' conflates a legitimate metaethical question (what GROUNDS moral facts? — see the moral-argument entry) with a slander (atheists aren't moral) that is false in observation and, per Romans 2, false in doctrine. 'It takes more faith to be an atheist' equivocates — the atheist means by 'faith' precisely what she rejects, so the line lands as a taunt, not an argument. All three substitute diagnosis of the person for engagement with the position. The entire posture of this section depends on refusing that substitution.

sources.name: Romans 2:14-15 (the text that forbids the trope)
SEP, 'Atheism and Agnosticism' (what atheists actually claim)
Pew Research, religious 'nones' and deconversion data
John Marriott's research on deconversion and church hurt

response: The skeptic's response is simply true and should be received as such: 'I don't secretly believe — I left slowly, honestly, and at real personal cost, and being told otherwise is being called a liar.' On morality: moral MOTIVATION and moral knowledge are demonstrably independent of metaethics — atheists donate kidneys and run soup kitchens, and Euthyphro-style questions show grounding puzzles cut at theists too. On 'more faith': defining the atheist's evidential standard as 'faith' is a word game that concedes the argument by changing the dictionary. Each rebuttal is correct; each trope, deployed, confirms the deconvert's suspicion that the church argues in bad faith.
responseSource: Any honest deconvert testimony; the standard atheist replies (e.g., in Oppy's and Antony's academic work on atheist morality)
rationale: Don't use — graded 'answered' because the skeptical rebuttals to all three tropes succeed, and in this case the Bible is on the skeptic's side of the exchange (Romans 2 predicts the moral atheist). Usage: engage arguments, never diagnose interlocutors; with deconverts especially, ask about their story before offering any case at all. This entry is the tonal keystone of the whole section.
context: 'You know God exists and you're suppressing it.' 'You just want to keep sinning.' 'Atheism takes more faith than Christianity.' Each of these tells the person in front of you that you are addressing a stereotype rather than them, and each one ends the conversation while feeling, to the speaker, like a point scored. This case is about why they fail even when the underlying theology is defensible — a claim about someone's inner motives is not something you can know, and they can tell.

title: 'They died for it' — the argument in the only form that works
claim: The disciples suffered and in several cases died rather than deny that they had seen Jesus alive. People will die for something they sincerely believe, but nobody dies for something they know they made up — and these particular people were in a position to know.
response: The skeptic's reply comes in three parts, and the first two are right. (1) Sincerity proves nothing about truth. The 9/11 hijackers died for their faith; so have Heaven's Gate members, Jim Jones's congregation, and martyrs of every religion on earth. Willingness to die establishes that a person believes what they are saying — nothing more. (2) The historical record for most of the apostles is very thin. Only one apostolic death is recorded in the New Testament: James son of Zebedee, beheaded by Herod Agrippa I around AD 44 (Acts 12:2). The vivid traditions — Thomas speared in India, Bartholomew flayed alive, Andrew on an X-shaped cross, Peter crucified upside down — come from apocryphal Acts written between the second and fourth centuries, which also contain talking animals and resurrected fish. Sean McDowell's The Fate of the Apostles (2015) is the most thorough treatment by a Christian scholar, and he grades the evidence honestly: he judges the martyrdoms of Peter, Paul, James son of Zebedee and James the brother of Jesus as historically well-established, John's death as probably natural, and most of the rest as possible but not demonstrable. (3) And even granting all of it, martyrdom establishes only that the disciples sincerely believed they had seen the risen Jesus — which skeptical scholars like Gerd Lüdemann already concede without difficulty, explaining the belief as visionary experience.

responseSource.name: Sean McDowell, The Fate of the Apostles (2015); Candida Moss, The Myth of Persecution (2013); Gerd Lüdemann, The Resurrection of Jesus

sources.name: Sean McDowell, The Fate of the Apostles (Routledge, 2015)
1 Clement 5 (c. AD 95) — on Peter and Paul's sufferings
Josephus, Antiquities 20.200 — the execution of James, the brother of Jesus
Tacitus, Annals 15.44 — the Neronian persecution
Candida Moss, The Myth of Persecution (HarperOne, 2013)

rationale: Graded contested because the popular version fails and the disciplined version holds, and the difference between them is everything. What survives scrutiny is a narrow, real point: the disciples were not in the position of ordinary religious martyrs. A Muslim martyr dies for a revelation he received on someone else's testimony; a Heaven's Gate member dies for a metaphysics nobody could check. The disciples are claiming to have eaten with a man they watched die — a claim about which they personally could not be honestly mistaken in the way a second-hand believer can. Either they saw something or they knew they hadn't. Paul is the sharpest case, because he was persecuting the movement and had every worldly reason not to join it, and 2 Corinthians 11 lists what it cost him in his own hand. So the argument does real work, but bounded work: it establishes sincerity, not truth. It rules out deliberate fraud — the 'they stole the body and made it up' theory — and it rules out nothing else. Present it that way, with the thin evidence for the ten conceded up front, and it is durable. Present it as 'all twelve apostles were tortured to death and none recanted' and you will meet someone who has read McDowell, and you will lose everything you said before it.
talk: Never say 'all twelve were martyred.' Say the narrow thing: **“I'm not arguing that dying for a belief makes it true — plenty of people have died for things that were false. I'm arguing these particular men were in a position to know whether they had made it up, and they behaved for the rest of their lives like men who hadn't.”** Then concede the evidence for most of them is late and thin, and name Paul, who was on the other side first.
context: 'They died for it' is one of the most-repeated arguments in Christian conversation, and in its usual form it does not work — people die for false beliefs constantly, which any skeptic will point out immediately. This case rescues the narrow version that does work. The disciples were not believing someone else's testimony about an event they never saw; they were claiming to have eaten with a man they watched die. That is a claim about which they could not be honestly mistaken in the way a second-hand believer can. It rules out deliberate fraud, and nothing more.

title: DON'T USE: 'all twelve apostles were martyred and not one recanted'
claim: A staple of sermons and tracts: every one of the twelve was tortured to death, and a single recantation would have ended Christianity — yet not one of them broke.
response: There is no ancient source that says this, and there never was. The New Testament records one apostolic death (James son of Zebedee, Acts 12:2). Peter and Paul's deaths in Rome are early and well-attested — 1 Clement, written around AD 95, speaks of their sufferings, and Tacitus describes Nero's persecution — but the specific details, including the upside-down cross, come from later tradition. For most of the others, the source is a body of apocryphal Acts composed from the second to the fourth century, texts that also feature a talking lion and a resurrected smoked fish. Early Christian tradition holds that John died of old age at Ephesus, which by itself falsifies the 'all twelve' claim. The 'not one recanted' half is worse: it is an argument from the absence of records nobody kept. We have no roster of who held firm because we have no reliable roster of what happened to most of them at all. Sean McDowell, writing as a Christian apologist specifically to defend this line of evidence, is the one who documents how little of it can be established.

responseSource.name: Sean McDowell, The Fate of the Apostles (2015) — a Christian scholar's own grading of the evidence

sources.name: Sean McDowell, The Fate of the Apostles (Routledge, 2015)
The Acts of Thomas (3rd c. apocryphal)
Eusebius, Church History 3.31 — John at Ephesus

rationale: Avoid because it overclaims a real argument into a false one, and because the correction is a single search away. The moment a skeptic checks Thomas or Bartholomew and finds a third-century romance, everything true you said about the crucifixion, the creed and Paul is retroactively suspect — you have taught them that you repeat things you have not verified. The fix is not to drop the evidence but to shrink the claim to what the sources carry: Peter, Paul, James son of Zebedee and James the brother of Jesus, the last of those attested by Josephus, who was not a Christian. Four well-documented deaths made in the strongest possible position of knowledge is a better argument than twelve legendary ones, precisely because it survives being checked.
talk: If you have used this one — and most of us have — say so: **“I used to say all twelve were martyred. That's not what the sources support, and I stopped saying it.”** Then give the four that hold. Nothing rebuilds credibility with a skeptic faster than a Christian correcting a Christian talking point unprompted.
context: 'All twelve apostles were tortured to death and not one recanted' is a sermon staple, and there is no ancient source that says it. The New Testament records one apostolic death; John is traditionally held to have died of old age; and the vivid traditions about the rest come from second-to-fourth-century romances that also feature talking animals. This case is graded from Sean McDowell's own research — an apologist who set out to defend this evidence and documented honestly how little of it can be established.
